inline.s: "No-thought is not a blank oblivion (this is beginningless ignorance)."

No-thought" is not blank oblivion. What is blank oblivion? It is to be like a piece of wood or stone, with not a single thought arising—what is called "the emptiness of blank oblivion." The emptiness of blank oblivion is the "concentration of the extinction of perception and feeling": the feeling and perception are extinguished, one accepts no information from the outside at all, and there is no mental activity whatsoever. This blank oblivion is "beginningless ignorance"—it is not a good thing, so do not mistake it for something good. There are people who pursue this, who worship this. Oh! So-and-so practices well—he can enter concentration and not move for a whole week. Hey! So-and-so is even better—for a whole month he does not move. Good heavens! So-and-so has already sat for three years! These are all cases of blank oblivion. Even if you could enter concentration for eighty-four thousand kalpas, at best you would only reach the "concentration of neither perception nor non-perception," which is still the world's meditative absorption, still turning within the six realms of samsara, not yet liberated. To become a Buddha is to cultivate into a living Buddha, vividly and vitally giving rise to the subtle, living wonder of function—it is not sitting dead-still without moving. What use is there in sitting dead-still and not moving?

In the Tang dynasty, Master Xuanzang traveled to India to seek the scriptures. As he reached the Himalayan region, he discovered a purple cloud spreading like a canopy over the mountain, and knew that a cultivator must dwell within. So everyone went searching. Up on the mountain there had once been a cave, but as the years passed trees fell and grass grew, and the cave mouth was buried. They searched and searched, until suddenly someone noticed what looked like a cave and began to dig there. Digging in, sure enough it was a cave, and there was a man sitting inside. Xuanzang's disciples said, "This man is dead; look, he is cold as ice, nothing but skin wrapped around a skeleton." Master Xuanzang felt his chest and found it still slightly warm, which showed he was not dead—the eighth consciousness had not yet departed. The eighth consciousness is the "warmth-life consciousness," and a little warmth remaining at the chest showed he still had a span of life. Xuanzang tapped the small gong, and the practitioner came out of his concentration. He opened his eyes and saw: "Ah! The Buddha has come, come to preach the Dharma to me." He had been sitting here waiting for Shakyamuni Buddha to appear in the world and preach to him, so when he saw Xuanzang he took him for Shakyamuni Buddhis coming to lead him and deliver him. Xuanzang said, "I am not Shakyamuni Buddha; the Buddha has long since passed into parinirvana." The Buddha's advent in the world was around the time of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, whereas Xuanzang lived in the Tang dynasty under Emperor Taizong (Li Shimin)—a very long time had passed. The practitioner wept: "Alas! I missed my chance. I was waiting for the Buddha to appear and deliver me, but he has already passed away." Xuanzang said, "Do not weep. The Buddha's Dharma is still in the world, and I am journeying to the Buddha-land to seek the true scriptures; in the future I will return to China and greatly revive the Buddha's Dharma. This body of yours is of no further use—you have sat for more than a thousand years (his concentration lasted more than a thousand years, not three years or five), so it can no longer be used. Change it for a new body! Make haste and take rebirth in China; and when you are grown, I too shall have returned. You must take rebirth in a great mansion with high towers and glazed tiles—do not go to a small place." So this practitioner took rebirth, entering the household of Yuchi Gong and becoming a young prince. This practitioner had entered concentration for well over a thousand years—his skill must have been excellent, right? No! This concentration of the extinction of perception and feeling is useless; it is like pressing down grass with a stone—when the stone is removed the grass grows again, and grows all the worse. When he grew up he was attached to appearances, and giving way to lust he brought disaster upon himself, and was cast into the ancestral temple to have his head cut off. Yuchi Gong was a meritorious minister whose family had been enfeoffed as princes; but before a prince could be beheaded, he was first thrown into the ancestral temple. Yet if he became a monk, he would not be beheaded, so he had no choice but to leave home as a monk. But he insisted on bringing women, a band, and all manner of delicacies, loading three carts full. People mocked him as the "monk of the three carts." Later, Xuanzang awakened him to his former life, and suddenly he understood, and let go of all "three carts." He was Xuanzang's great disciple, Master Kuiji, who later accomplished much and became the second-generation patriarch of the Dharmalaksana (Faxiang) school.

Therefore, we must practice vividly and vitally; sitting dead-still is of no use. True concentration is to be unconfused when confronted by objects of experience. Whatever happens, my mind is undisturbed; what has womanly beauty appears before me, my mind does not move; no matter how much treasure comes, it cannot move my heart. This is true concentration. If, when confronting an object, the mind stirs and you press it down again, that is not true concentration either—there is still a mind of arising and ceasing! Why is a first-stage arhat still reborn seven times among the gods and seven times among humans? Because he still has a mind of arising and ceasing. A thought comes, and you immediately become alert and extinguish it—this too is the mind of arising and ceasing; so long as there is arising and ceasing, one returns again and again to humans and gods. In our practice we must make genuine effort, guarding the true mind without loss at every moment. No-thought is not blank oblivion—understanding this clearly is extremely important.
"And it is further different from the ordinary worldly person."

It is also different from the heterodox and the ordinary. To seek the Dharma outside the mind is to be heterodox. The heterodox also speak of no-thought, but their no-thought is dead. The breath practice of the ordinary person does not leave attachment behind; he too speaks of no-thought. But his no-thought is all the more not genuine no-thought. He is attached to the breath—where the breath goes, now to the crown, now to the elixir field, now to the yongquan point, the great circulation, the small circulation, and so on. Can these be counted as no-thought? So the no-thought of which we speak is different from the no-thought of the heterodox and the ordinary; it has nothing whatsoever to do with their practices.
"Through not having awakened one begins to awaken; the initial awakening is the child-light born of the original awakening, and it merges with the mother-light."

When we all practice, it is "through not having awakened that one begins to awaken." Formerly we did not awaken; through entering the path and practicing, we now begin to awaken. The Dharma I am preaching to you now is precisely so that you may begin to awaken. The wisdom-light emitted by the initial awakening "is the child-light born of the original awakening." Original awakening is our Buddha-nature. Original awakening is the "mother-light," initial awakening is the "child-light," and the child-light is born of the mother-light, just as a mother gives birth to a son. "And it merges with the mother-light" means that initial awakening merges with original awakening. When mother and child merge, one attains the path; if mother and child do not merge, one cannot attain the path. You must contemplate at every moment and not cling to external objects of experience—this is the process of initial awakening merging with original awakening. When initial awakening and original awakening become one, that is the mother-child merging. For example, when we practice the Heart-Mantra (Xinzhongxin) method, the fourth seal is the "Tathagata mother-seal." The mother can give birth to the child, and mother and child merginge, thereby realizing the great path. The Pure Land school speaks the same way: "The Tathagatas of the ten directions think upon sentient beings with compassion, as a mother remembers her son. If the son runs away, what use is the mother's remembering? If the son remembers his mother as the mother remembers him, then through every birth, mother and child are never far apart." These words were spoken by Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva. When we recite the Buddha's name, the Buddha is the mother and we are the child; the Buddha is always at every moment leading us on. If the son remembers the mother, as the mother remembers the son, then mother and child merge, and the attainment of the path comes swiftly. All twelve sections of the Tripitaka are breathed from the same nose. Grasp this essential principle—truly understand it, and all twelve sections of the Tripitaka become clear. If one does not grasp the essential principle and quotes lines out of context, everything is shattered and lost, leaving one at a loss. Therefore, to see the nature at every moment—this is most important.
"Though one establishes the view of the essential nature, it is not what can be realized without practice."

Even though we have established the "view of the essential nature" and have the correct understanding, clearly knowing what the nature is, and knowing that one must cultivate with this nature in order to attain the path—nevertheless, this does not mean there is no practice. If one does not cultivate the path, can one realize the path? No! Hence it is said, "Nor is it what can be realized without practice"—it is not as if, without practicing, one can realize the path.
"Gold-bearing sand possesses the substance of gold, but is not yet gold; the labor of smelting and refining is required."

Gold-bearing sand is sand that contains gold, that is, a gold-bearing ore. "Gold-bearing sand possesses the substance of gold" means that, in essence, the gold-bearing sand contains gold and has the quality of gold. "But it is not yet gold" means that though it contains gold, it is not yet pure gold; there are still impurities such as sand mixed in. "The labor of smelting and refining is required" means that a process of smelting or refinement is necessary, to remove the sand and other impurities before it can become pure gold. This is a metaphor for the fact that all sentient beings (the gold-bearing sand), though possessed of the Tathagata's wisdom and virtuous marks and fully endowed with Buddha-nature (possessing the quality of gold), still have ignorance and false imaginings and attachments—they are not yet Buddhas of the fruit-ground! In other words, though sentient beings have Buddha-nature, they are not yet Buddhas (but are not yet gold). A process of practice is required (the labor of smelting and refining is required), suddenly to break through ignorance and further wipe away all false imaginings and attachments, before one can become a Buddha. This passage, taking the smelting of gold ore as a simile, is intended to emphasize the importance of practice. How then does one practice? See the following text.

"The three gates of practice: the practice of body, to leave all activities—such as deeds in the world that bring no benefit and other world-transcending practices as well—and merely abiding at ease, expansive and calm, letting the body dwell in stillness."

The three gates of practice refer to the practice of body, the practice of speech, and the practice of mind. The esoteric school emphasizes the three secrets—body, speech, and mind. The three gates of practice likewise refer to body, speech, and mind. The first is the "practice of body," which is the method of cultivation established on this body of flesh and blood. "To leave all activities" means to be far from all manner of doing—"deeds in the world that bring no benefit": things in the world that are of no benefit, such as playing mahjong; this brings no benefit and squanders and wastes the precious time of life. Among you, those fond of playing mahjong are perhaps not a few, and you will even use "we are short one player" as an excuse, going daily at it four-handed, fighting it out several rounds. That will not do! Deeds of no benefit must not be done. Not doing the world's unbeneficial deeds is itself practice—the practice of body. "And other world-transcending practices as well": there are many world-transcending methods of practice. If today you cultivate this and tomorrow that, it will not do either. You must enter deeply into one method, upholding one Dharma and carrying it through to the end. Today you hear Zhang San say this Dharma is good and so cultivate it; tomorrow you hear Li Si say that Dharma is good and go cultivate that instead. Though all these are the wondrous Dharma that transcends the world, changing back and forth like this will bear no fruit, because your mind is not focused and cannot respond to the wondrous Dharma. Moreover, many dharmas are of no benefit. For instance, there is a mantra by which one can bore a hole in a knife—this is a dharman of no benefit, of no use for liberation. You see that it can bore a hole in a knife and are delighted—"Good, I'll cultivate this one." What use is there in cultivating that?

I once heard a monk tell of his own circumstances for leaving home: before becoming a monk he practiced boxing, learning boxing and the sword from his maternal uncle. One day, at the border of Sichuan, he saw two young Tibetan lamas smoking opium. He could not stand it, so he went to intervene: "Hey! You are monks, so how can you smoke opium?" The young lamas said, "Never mind that we smoke opium; we have magic powers." He asked, "What magic powers do you have?" Seeing that he carried a knife, the lamas said, "Strike me with that knife you carry—I will recite a mantra and you will not be able to cut me." Finding this very novel, he at once asked, "Is there really such a method?" The lamas replied, "Of course there is; if you don't believe me, just try it. But first let me finish smoking my opium." After a while they had finished, and said, "Come, I shall recite the mantra; you strike." Actually he dared not truly strike—the knife was very sharp, and if he cut off a hand it would be hard to resolve. So he struck with the back of the blade, and the knife bounced up. "Hey! How did you knock my knife up like that?" The lama said, "Even if you strike with the blade, I am not afraid." "Truly not afraid?" "Of course not." "If it gets cut off, I won't take responsibility!" "You needn't take responsibility; go ahead and strike." This time he really struck with the blade, and again the knife bounced up. He was convinced and thought, "The Buddha's Dharma truly is wonderful, better than this skill I have trained in." It was on account of this circumstance that he took up the Buddha's Dharma. But this in fact is a dharman of no benefit; having learned it, it is of no use.

Merely abiding at ease, expansive and calm, letting the body dwell in stillness." Only by abiding at ease, expansive and calm, letting the body dwell in stillness, without any obstruction—not tense and bustling—is this achieved. The Heart Sutra says: "Because there is nothing to be attached to, there is no fear, and, far from inverted dream-thoughts, one reaches ultimate nirvana." If there is attachment, there is fear and inverted dream-thoughts. Being without attachment, the mind is utterly empty, and the breast becomes broad and even. Hence "the noble person is broad and magnanimous; the small person is forever anxious." The small person is always fretting over gain and loss, forever distressed and unable to get through the day; the noble person's breast is open and even, at ease and free. Pay attention, all of you: to abide at ease, expansive and calm, letting the body dwell in stillness—this is the practice of body. If in your heart you are always fretting over gain and loss, then you are not in accord with it. At ease, expansive and calm, letting the body dwell in stillness, with no afflictions in the heart, no cares dangling—always even-tempered and placid, light-hearted and joyful—then the body will be well and illness will little arise. Dwell thus in the world, and only then can you apply effort in the Dharma. This is the practice of body.
"The practice of speech: unbeneficial worldly talk and mantras and recitations alike are stopped; be still as a valley."
The second gate of the three is the practice of speech, the cultivation pertaining to talk and conversation.

Telling jokes, flattering someone, disparaging something—these worldly idle words are all of no benefit to the practice of the path of liberation; they are all unbeneficial worldly speech. Arguing right and wrong and the long and short of someone or something is even more frivolous talk. In the Black Sect of Tibetan esoteric traditions, many mantras are not for the path of liberation but for working on others—these are unbeneficial mantras and recitations. These things should not be spoken, should not be recited. "Unbeneficial worldly talk and mantras and recitations alike are stopped": in studying the Buddha's Dharma and practicing the path of liberation, we must enter deeply into one method; do not foolishly dabble in other things. Do not speak the world's unbeneficial words, and do not recite unbeneficial mantras or liturgical recitations. We should attain the "three few-nesses": few matters in the heart, few words in the mouth, and little food in the belly. People have a bad habit: once they have finished their tasks and have a moment of leisure, they go on and on about Zhang San, Li Si, and Wang Er Mazi. In practicing the path of liberation, that will not do. Would it not be better to be silent? "Be still as a valley"—do not speak much, and let the heart be still and quiet, like a deep, tranquil mountain valley. "A quiet valley's echo answers the evening mist." If you have a question to ask me, I shall answer you in detail and without any irritation; when there is no question, I do not deliberate or discriminate; let the heart be empty and open—"the great void drinks in the light, and the distant is consumed."

"The practice of mind: leaving behind frivolous theorizing, deliberation, and comparing and imagining; even visualization and mental application also cease. (Just when the mind is applied, just then it is applied with no mind.)"
The third gate of the three is the practice of mind, the cultivation pertaining to thought and consciousness.

What use is it to hold in the heart a whole set of empty theories, unrelated to the path of liberation, that one cannot put down? Analyzing them and reasoning them out is "frivolous theorizing"; thinking about them and evaluating them is "deliberation." One should "leave behind frivolous theorizing, deliberation, and comparing and imagining": let the heart be utterly empty and clean, far from frivolous theorizing and deliberation, and also far from comparing and imagining. To take every single thing and compare it—compare what? Whether I am better or you are better, whether I am the longer or you are the longer. This state of mind is not even, and is precisely false discrimination; this "comparing and imagining" must all the more be left behind.

Even visualization and mental application also cease." Visualization is a method of practice, as we have already mentioned. Thinking of something is still a cultivation with deliberate activity. For instance, "visualization-recitation of the Buddha": imagine Amitabha Buddha above my head, or contemplate that I myself am Amitabha Buddha. Visualization is always mental application, that is, deliberately stirring the thought consciousness into activity. Even this visualization, even this mental application, must stop. It is enough simply to contemplate well: when a thought arises, see it; having seen it, pay it no heed and do not run after it. Visualization is a gradual method; after visualization succeeds, one must still apply further effort to break through the image formed before one can see the nature. My teacher (Master Wang Xianglu) used this simile: suppose a large sore breaks out on the body, and medicine is used to treat it; then the sore's opening shrinks and shrinks and shrinks again, until at last it contracts into a small opening, even into a point. All the rest is healed over, and only this one point remains—this is a simile for the success of visualization. But this one point is still a sore! If it is not removed, it will break out again later. Hence one must further break through the image formed, and only then can one rest once and for all, and only then is it genuine realization of the Dharmakaya. If the image is not broken, the nature cannot manifest. That is why the practice of visualization must cross an extra threshold. All esoteric methods with images must cross an extra threshold, and in the end must break the image. How is the image broken? One must still make further effort: contemplate this image larger and larger, larger, larger—until it is boundless, and the image is gone. Or, conversely, contemplate it smaller and smaller, smaller, smaller—until there is nothing at all. One is the enlarging, the other the shrinking—in this way one breaks it. After the image is broken, one sees the nature, but has crossed an extra threshold. The Great Seal (Mahamudra) is the most direct Great Vehicle mind-nature Dharma-gate; it does not require these procedures. Hence it is said, "Even visualization and mental application also cease." The Great Seal does not take this road and does not cross these thresholds one by one. A thought arises and at once one sees it; having seen it, pay it no heed, and simply guard the true mind.

The phrase in parentheses is excerpted from a gatha of Chan Master Lanzong, to serve as a commentary on the "practice of mind." Master Lanzong's gatha is excellent, everyone likes to quote it; most quote four lines: "Just when the mind is applied, just then it is applied with no mind; applied with no mind, and ever applied, it is in truth applied in nothing." The complete gatha has eight lines: "Just when the mind is applied, just then it is applied with no mind. To expound names and marks in a roundabout way is toil; to speak directly is not heavy. Applied with no mind, and ever applied, it is in truth applied in nothing. Now when we speak of the place of no-mind, it is not different from a mind." While making effort and applying the mind, yet one finds no thought that can arise—this is "just when the mind is applied, just then it is applied with no mind." To go roundabout and talk at length of Buddhist names and marks exhausts the mind and labor; to point directly to the source of the mind and say nothing else is not so tedious, not so heavy. This is "to expound names and marks in a roundabout way is toil; to speak directly is not heavy." The great path has no form and the true mind no mark; though without form and mark, it is nevertheless functioning at every moment and in every place; though all things and affairs are its wondrous function, yet to seek its very self one can never get it. This is "applied with no mind, and ever applied, it is in truth applied in nothing." Now that we point directly to this "no-mind" and speak of it directly, it is again not different from "mind"—that is, "now when we speak of the place of no-mind, it is not different from a mind."

blocks.text: 8. Directly Realizing the Unsurpassed Way of Right Awakening

inline.s: "From the crown of the head to the soles of the feet, empty as a bamboo tube. The mind equals the void; utterly transcending all discrimination, it leaves behind dullness, agitation, and blank oblivion, and attains equanimity, sustaining, watchfulness, and stillness. Luminous and clear, without grasping or rejecting, without attachment, it abides in the original wondrous, luminous, pure substance of nature—this is the concentration of the Great Seal."

From the crown of the head to the soles of the feet, empty as a bamboo tube": from the top of the head to the soles of the feet, empty like a bamboo tube—the whole body and mind are utterly without a single thing. Look at that bamboo tube: set it floating on water and it drifts along with the current, bending where the water bends; whether high or low, whether sinking or floating, it does not care. A wave knocks it under, and at once it floats up again, sinking and floating according to conditions. One who has accomplished the practice is like this: "following conditions, expansive and at large, entrusting oneself to the sinking and floating; transforming into spring mud that nourishes the flowers."

The mind equals the void; utterly transcending all discrimination": the breast should be as vast as the void, not distinguishing beautiful from ugly, able to contain everything within. Within the void are all things; when high towers and great mansions rise up, the void does not say it cannot hold them. When you tear the houses down, the void is not broader; when you enlarge the houses, the void is not narrower. When a plane flies up, the void pays no mind; when black clouds gather and thunder flashes, the void has never stirred in sound or color, it does not care. Our true mind was originally like the void and has never stirred. Now, taking hold of the true mind, we should "make the mind equal the void, utterly transcending all discrimination." Whatever happens, I do not concern myself. The void can contain all things, and I too can contain all things. The worlds of the ten directions are within the void, and the worlds of the ten directions are also in my heart. Nirvana with no abode—one can go to any place, not confined to a single one. Make the breast as vast as the void, as broad as the void, as non-abiding as the void, as unattached as the void. Within the void there is no thing, yet nothing at all obstructs it. "Utterly transcending all discrimination" means to transcend and sever all thought of discriminating, grasping, and rejecting. Discrimination, grasping, and rejecting are all false thoughts, and all false thoughts must be severed.

Leaving behind dullness, agitation, and blank oblivion, and attaining equanimity, sustaining, watchfulness, and stillness." "Leaving behind" means to depart from. "Dullness" is mental torpor and dozing. "The lazy ox has many sleep-matters on the road": it is like the lazy ox—do not get it onto the road and sleep doesn't come, but once on the road it starts dozing. Some people are fine when they don't sit, but the moment they sit in meditation they grow dull and fall into snoring sleep. "Agitation" is restlessness, many false thoughts. Sitting there one's thoughts jump about every which way. To practice like that is absolutely not acceptable. We must be neither dull nor agitated, but neither may we fall into blank oblivion. Blank oblivion is to have no right mindfulness even—like a piece of wood or stone—and that too is unacceptable. We must be clearly aware, with right mindfulness dazzlingly present. We always speak of contemplating the mind, contemplating the mind—contemplate and hold it there, but do not fall into blank oblivion; right mindfulness must still be present.

Equanimity means evenness, sustaining means holding evenly; watchfulness is contemplation, is wisdom; stillness is tranquility, is concentration. What is called "the sustaining of concentration and wisdom with equanimity" is that stillness and watchfulness are held in even measure, with neither one high nor the other low. It is not more watchfulness and less stillness, or more stillness and less watchfulness, but equal measure, held evenly—at once clear and aware, and at once still and unmoving; at once still and unmoving, and at once clear and aware. Concentration and wisdom are one substance; within concentration there is wisdom, and within wisdom there is concentration. Only when they are one substance can they be sustained in equanimity.

Luminous and clear, without grasping or rejecting, without attachment": the true mind is luminous and clear—its spiritual light shines alone and utterly separates from the dust of the sense-organs; the spiritual light still shines and is clearly aware; there is no grasping, no rejecting, and still less attachment. It is keen and bright, like grasping a gourd floating on water—grasp it left and it turns left, grasp it right and it turns right; you can never catch it. Earlier it was likened to "empty as a bamboo tube"; the bamboo tube and the gourd alike are inexpressibly luminous floating on water, uncatchable. It is only without grasping, rejecting, and attachment that one can be luminous and clear. Grasping, rejecting, and attachment must all be utterly put down.

Abiding in the original wondrous, luminous, pure substance of nature—this is the concentration of the Great Seal." Where does it abide? It abides in "the original wondrous, luminous, pure nature-substance." The true mind is originally of boundless wondrous function, originally of immeasurable luminosity, originally pure and undefiled—this is the nature-substance of the true mind. To abide on the true-mind substance is precisely "non-abiding." Because the true-mind substance has no form—how can what has no form abide? It abides by way of "non-abiding," and this is "the concentration of the Great Seal." Nowadays people often speak of the Great Seal; what is the Great Seal? The true-mind substance is the Great Seal. Have you all understood? Do not ask again how the Great Seal mudra is formed—is it the left hand or the right? The true-mind substance is the Great Seal. Boundless wondrous function, immeasurable luminosity, pure and undefiled, and abiding through non-abiding—this is the concentration of the Great Seal.
"Cultivating constantly in this way, suddenly, in an instant, as when a lamp lights in a dark room, the bright light opens up and shines."

What I spoke of just now is the three gates of practice: body, speech, and mind. "Cultivating constantly in this way"—practicing constantly like this, and then suddenly the spirit leaps with brilliance. "Suddenly, in an instant, as when a lamp lights in a dark room, the bright light opens up and shines": in an instant, as when a lamp is lit in a dark room, the light of the mind bursts forth and it all opens wide in brightness. What is this? This is awakening—the bottom of the bucket falling out, the original being opened. This is the opening of a great treasury of light, the mind-light brightly illumining heaven and earth, and the worlds of the ten directions all complete within your heart. If you have not reached this point, then even if there is some apprehension, it can only count as "a single line of the mind opening." Only one thread of brightness—that cannot count. Arriving at this point, it is like a great explosion: with a "boom," the void shatters to powder and the great earth sinks level; self, others, and the whole world all vanish without remainder. When does this happen? One cannot know; when the time and causes are ripe, with a "pop" it breaks open. There is no fixed place, not necessarily in some particular spot. Must it be at home? Must it be at the time of sitting in meditation? Not necessarily! Sometimes it is on the road, sometimes in a public place, sometimes within a dream—in any of these it can manifest. When the effort is ripe and the time and causes arrive, it naturally manifests; this is called "when the water comes, the channel is formed." The stream surges in, and the channel is naturally completed. If there is no water, the channel does not count as completed. So long as you practice constantly in this way, when the time and causes arrive, suddenly it comes. This "suddenly" is very important—it is not fixed to some particular time. If there were a fixed time, you would have a mind of waiting. One must not "await awakening with the mind"! You cannot wait for awakening; the moment there is a mind of waiting, it is spoiled—it will never come, and you will never awaken. Those of us who practice the Heart-Mantra method, take note: do not count your sittings! Do not keep muttering, "I have already sat so many hundred sittings; how many more before I reach the thousand?" Do not count! Put it down at once; counting the number is not permissible—this is a mind of waiting, and it must not be! The scene of breaking open erupts suddenly; when the effort is mature, it naturally erupts. Do not have a mind of waiting; just practice diligently! When you hear me say "a boom," do not suppose it is like hearing the sound of a thunderclap. It is not; it is only such a realm of experience, and you feel a "boom," but no one else can hear it. The most important thing is to practice well. Practice, and it will naturally come; do not practice, and it will not come. If you anticipate it, wait for it, with this mind of waiting, it will not come.
"The nirvana-nature, the wisdom-light of the co-nascent original awakening, manifests in its entirety. One directly realizes the unsurpassed Way of right awakening."
The nirvana-nature" —what is it? It is the nature that is originally neither born nor extinguished.

The wisdom-light of the co-nascent original awakening." Co-nascent is that which arises together with our life. Original awakening is to be originally awake, not that one begins to be awake at some particular time. The wisdom-light of the co-nascent original awakening is the wisdom-light that is originally inherent in the self-mind, that has existed from the very beginning.

Manifests in its entirety"—it manifests completely, with nothing at all hidden, that is, one personally sees and realizes it. Now, I speak and you listen; you take it in through the ears, entering by the gate of the ear. "What enters through the gate is not the family treasure." You must yourself realize this point—with a "pop," open the original and personally realize it once—only then does it count.

One directly realizes the unsurpassed Way of right awakening"—at once one realizes the highest, unsurpassed great Way of right awakening—unsurpassed, right, and equal awakening. At this time you will know: to speak of birth and death, to discourse on nirvana, on whether it is thorough or not, whether ultimate or not—all such talk is frivolous theorizing! At this time you can teach by living example, and toward sentient beings with affinities, "cause them all to enter the nirvana of no remainder and be delivered."
Everyone! Apply effort! Advance and strive onward! Apply effort diligently! Advance and strive!
